The Redcoat (Sargocentron rubrum) is a moderately sized squirrelfish that inhabits coral reefs and rocky substrates throughout the Red Sea and Indo-Pacific region. Field surveys of adult populations indicate that individuals attain a maximum total length of 32 centimeters [Li = 32 centimeters], a dimension that places this species among the medium-bodied members of the Holocentridae family. This ultimate size is achieved gradually over several years of somatic growth, with most recaptured individuals showing asymptotic length increments after the fifth year. Data from otolith-based age validation studies suggest that the length-at-age relationship follows a decelerating trajectory typical of reef fishes, with the majority of structural growth completed by the time the fish reaches sexual maturity. The relatively modest terminal size likely reflects energetic constraints imposed by the species' nocturnal foraging strategy and the structural complexity of its preferred microhabitat, where crevice-dwelling imposes a ceiling on body dimensions. Comparative data from congeneric species indicate that Sargocentron rubrum is intermediate in size between the smaller Sargocentron microstoma and the larger Sargocentron spiniferum, which can exceed 45 centimeters in total length.

Reproductive development in Sargocentron rubrum begins when individuals reach a total length at puberty of 14.7 centimeters [Lp = 14.7 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to the onset of gonadal maturation and the first detectable vitellogenic activity in females. At this size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 51 grams [Wwp = 51 grams], based on length-weight regressions derived from specimens collected across the central Red Sea. Fish approaching this developmental milestone exhibit a pronounced acceleration in gonad somatic index, with circulating steroid hormone levels rising several weeks before the first histological signs of oocyte recruitment. The body mass at which puberty occurs represents roughly one-tenth of the ultimate wet weight of 513 grams [Wwi = 513 grams] recorded from fully grown adults, a pattern consistent with the general life-history expectation that maturation occurs well before the attainment of asymptotic size in iteroparous teleosts. Field observations indicate that pubertal fish often aggregate near shallow reef flats during the late spring months, presumably in preparation for their first seasonal spawning event.

The reproductive output of Sargocentron rubrum is strongly modulated by water temperature, with field measurements conducted at 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C] revealing that spawning females produce approximately 1,770 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1,770 eggs per spawning event] across the peak of the breeding season. This high fecundity is sustained by an ovarian morphology characterized by asynchronous oocyte development, allowing continuous batch spawning over a protracted reproductive period. The associated spawning frequency under these thermal conditions is estimated at roughly one spawning event per day [F_R_i = roughly one spawning event per day], resulting in a total daily reproductive output that ranks among the highest recorded for similarly sized holocentrids. The elevated temperature of 28.1 °C appears to optimize both the rate of vitellogenesis and the efficiency of yolk protein incorporation into developing oocytes. Females in cooler waters, below 25 °C, exhibit a marked reduction in both batch fecundity and spawning frequency, suggesting that the species' reproductive schedule is finely attuned to stable warm-water environments typical of equatorial reef systems.

Early life history in Sargocentron rubrum proceeds rapidly under the warm conditions typical of its tropical habitat. Fertilised eggs, which measure approximately 0.8 millimeters in diameter, hatch after an incubation period of 3.5 days [ab = 3.5 days] at a temperature of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C], with chorionase secretion triggered by the accumulation of hatching enzymes within the perivitelline space. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva possesses a wet weight at birth of 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], a value derived from the geometric relationship between egg diameter and spherical volume. This minimal initial mass necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding, as the endotrophic larval stage is sustained solely by the endogenous yolk reserves that are absorbed within the first few days following eclosion. The timing of chorion rupture and subsequent larval emergence appears tightly synchronized with the nocturnal activity patterns of the species, likely reducing predation risk on the vulnerable prolarvae during their initial dispersal in the water column. Laboratory rearing trials have confirmed that the hatching success rate exceeds 85 percent under stable thermal regimes near 28 °C.

Longevity records for Sargocentron rubrum indicate a maximum lifespan of 15 years [am = 15 years] when maintained at a stable temperature of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C], based on mark-recapture data from a long-term monitoring program in the Gulf of Aqaba. This lifespan, equivalent to approximately 5,475 days, places the species among the longer-lived members of the family Holocentridae, with individuals commonly surviving for more than a decade in undisturbed reef habitats. The relationship between body size and longevity in this species follows the general positive allometry observed across teleost fishes, yet the maximum age recorded here notably exceeds predictions based solely on asymptotic length. Senescent individuals, typically those beyond the age of 12 years, show reduced gonadal output and increased incidence of spinal curvature and fin erosion. The ecological implications of this extended lifespan include a prolonged reproductive window that buffers against recruitment failures in poor environmental years. The largest documented adult, weighing 513 grams [Wwi = 513 grams], was captured at an estimated age of 14 years, underscoring the gradual nature of late-life growth in this species.
